title: Bombs fall on Helsinki

facts.text: The Soviet invasion of Finland began on 30 November 1939. The main attack opened at 6:50 a.m. with an artillery barrage on the Karelian Isthmus.

Helsinki's first air raid sirens sounded at 9:15 a.m. Five minutes later three Soviet SB bombers appeared, aiming for Malmi airfield. Clouds made them miss, and their bombs fell in residential districts.
A second wave came in mid morning and bombed the island fortresses and naval air base in the bay. The American minister in Helsinki cabled Washington about both morning raids that day.
The worst raid came between 3:00 and 4:20 p.m. Bombs hit the city centre between Hietalahti and the Kamppi bus station, and a wing of the Technical University was left blazing.
Finnish authorities later put the afternoon raid alone at 61 dead and 120 wounded, the heaviest toll of any single raid in the war. Yle counts 91 people killed in the day's raids.

Soviet state radio said the Finnish reports of air raids were false and that Soviet planes had dropped only bread on Helsinki. The claim of food drops for starving Finns was pinned on Foreign Minister Vyacheslav Molotov.

The Finns answered with sarcasm. They called the Soviet cluster bombs "Molotov's bread baskets" and named their petrol bottle bomb, used against Soviet tanks, the Molotov cocktail: a drink to go with the food.

Finland's armed forces were led by Marshal Carl Gustaf Emil Mannerheim, born on 4 June 1867 and 72 years old when the war began. He commanded them for the next five years and later served as president.
The Red Army came with about half a million troops. Finland fought on alone until the Moscow Peace of 13 March 1940, when it gave up the Karelian Isthmus and other land.
Finland lost about 26,000 dead or missing. Soviet dead and missing are put at between 126,000 and 168,000.

declassified.fact: On the first day of the war Finland's Foreign Minister, Eljas Erkko, went on the radio in English to speak directly to the American people. That same afternoon one of the buildings bombed in central Helsinki housed the Soviet Union's own embassy.

body:
Moscow radio told the world its planes had dropped only bread on Helsinki. In Helsinki, the city centre was on fire.

30 November 1939. The Soviet invasion of Finland began that morning. Helsinki's first sirens sounded at 9:15 a.m., and the worst raid came between 3:00 and 4:20 p.m., when bombs hit the city centre and left a wing of the Technical University blazing. Yle counts 91 people killed in the day's raids.

The Finns answered with sarcasm. They called the Soviet cluster bombs Molotov's bread baskets, and named their petrol bottle bomb the Molotov cocktail, a drink to go with the food.

Finland fought on alone until March 1940.
